blocks.text: Exact match is the strictest, simplest automated evaluation metric available, it scores a model output as correct only when it is identical, or identical after light normalization, to a known correct gold answer, with no partial credit for close but imperfect responses.
This topic covers where exact match is genuinely the right metric to use, how normalization affects its behavior, and why it becomes unreliable outside a fairly narrow set of tasks.
1. What Exact Match Actually Checks

blocks.alt: A model answer and a gold answer are compared with an exact string compare

blocks.text: Exact match compares a model output directly against a known correct gold answer, scoring one if the strings match and zero otherwise, no partial credit exists between those two outcomes.
2. Binary Scoring, No In-Between

blocks.alt: Identical strings score 1, anything else scores 0

blocks.text: Unlike BLEU, ROUGE, or BERTScore, all covered in earlier topics, which produce a continuous score reflecting degrees of similarity, exact match produces a strictly binary outcome per example, correct or incorrect, then reports the fraction of correct examples across a full evaluation set as the final metric.
3. Where Exact Match Fits Well

blocks.alt: Classification tasks fit exact match well, open ended generation tasks fit it poorly

blocks.text: Exact match works well for tasks with a single, well defined correct answer, classification labels, short factual question answering, multiple choice selection, structured extraction tasks, where genuine correctness really is binary and there is little room for valid variation in phrasing.
4. Normalization Before Comparing

blocks.alt: Raw model output gets normalized for case, whitespace, and punctuation before comparing

blocks.text: Most practical exact match implementations apply light normalization first, lowercasing text, stripping extra whitespace, removing trailing punctuation, since without this step, trivial formatting differences that do not reflect any real error would still count as a mismatch.
5. Exact Match vs Token F1

blocks.alt: Exact match is strict while token F1 gives partial credit

blocks.text: Many question answering benchmarks report exact match alongside a softer token-level F1 score, which gives partial credit for overlapping words even when the full answer string does not match exactly, exact match tends to be the stricter, more conservative of the two, penalizing answers that are substantively correct but phrased slightly differently.

blocks.text: 6. Where Exact Match Becomes Misleading

blocks.alt: Numeric answer 4 matches gold but the word four gets no raw string match

blocks.text: A correct answer expressed in a different valid format, a number written as a digit versus spelled out as a word, a date written in a different order, scores as entirely wrong under raw exact match even though it is substantively correct, a common source of misleadingly low scores unless the evaluation pipeline accounts for these equivalent forms.

blocks.title: Format mismatches are the most common exact match failure mode
blocks.content: Careful benchmark evaluation pipelines often normalize numbers, dates, and known equivalent phrasings before comparing, since raw exact match without this handling systematically undercounts correct answers.

blocks.text: 7. Why Exact Match Fails for Open Ended Generation

For open ended tasks like summarization, creative writing, or extended explanation, there is rarely a single correct string, exact match would score nearly every genuinely good response as wrong, making it entirely unsuitable outside tasks with a narrow, well defined answer space.
8. Why Exact Match Remains Useful Despite Its Strictness

blocks.alt: Exact match score is fast, cheap, and unambiguous

blocks.text: Despite its limitations, exact match remains valuable specifically because it is fast, cheap, and completely unambiguous, no model or embedding computation is required, and there is no disagreement possible about what the score means, a genuinely useful property for benchmark evaluation covered in the next topic.
9. Combining Exact Match With Other Metrics

For tasks that sit between fully open ended and fully structured, reporting exact match alongside a softer metric like token F1 or BERTScore, covered in an earlier topic, often gives a more complete picture than either alone, strict correctness alongside a sense of how close near misses actually are.
Worked Example

A team fine-tuning a model for structured data extraction, pulling a specific field value out of documents, uses exact match as their primary evaluation metric, since the task genuinely has one correct answer per example and near misses are not meaningfully useful.

Early results show a surprisingly low exact match score, investigation reveals the model is often extracting the substantively correct value but formatted slightly differently, a date written as day-month-year instead of the gold answer month-day-year format, adding a normalization step that accounts for equivalent date formats immediately raises the measured score to reflect the model actual performance.
Common Mistakes

items: Using exact match for open ended generation tasks where many different phrasings are equally valid
Skipping normalization and letting trivial formatting differences count as full errors
Not accounting for equivalent answer formats, like numbers versus spelled out words, before comparing
Reporting exact match as the only metric when a softer partial credit metric would give a more complete picture

blocks.text: Practice

For a task you are familiar with, decide whether exact match would be an appropriate primary metric, and if not, identify what kind of partial credit or softer metric, from this module topics, would better fit that task answer space.
Key Takeaway

Exact match scores a model output as strictly correct or incorrect against a gold answer, a fast, cheap, and unambiguous metric that fits tasks with a single well defined correct answer well, but becomes misleading without careful normalization and is entirely unsuitable for open ended generation tasks where valid answers can take many different forms.
